subsystems.name: Sensing
subsystems.role: measures the things the thermostat reasons about.
parts: occupancy sensor (passive infrared, or radar in newer units)

subsystems.name: Control and switching
subsystems.role: closes and opens the low-voltage circuits that tell the furnace, boiler or air conditioner what to do.
parts: terminal block for standard wires (call for heat, call for cool, fan, common)

subsystems.name: Power supply
subsystems.role: runs the electronics from the HVAC control transformer or a battery.
parts: power-stealing circuit for installs without a common wire

subsystems.name: Compute and firmware
subsystems.role: runs the learning and scheduling logic and keeps the equipment safe.

subsystems.name: Connectivity and cloud
subsystems.role: lets the unit be set up, monitored and adjusted remotely, and drawn on for grid programmes.

subsystems.name: Enclosure and interface
subsystems.role: the part a person actually touches.
parts: mounting plate matching common wall-box spacing

subsystems.name: Remote sensors (optional)
subsystems.role: extend sensing into bedrooms and living rooms so control follows people, not just the hallway.
parts: wireless link to the main unit

buildSteps.title: Define compatibility
buildSteps.detail: Decide which heating and cooling systems to support — gas furnace, boiler, air conditioner, heat pump — and which control wires they expose, since a missing common wire changes the whole power design.

buildSteps.title: Design the board and power stage
buildSteps.detail: Lay out sensing, computing and switching on one printed circuit board and design the supply so the unit can run from the 24 V AC control transformer, or trickle-charge by briefly drawing current through the heating or cooling circuit where no common wire exists.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the sensors
buildSteps.detail: Temperature sensing is only useful if it is accurate, so each thermistor is characterised and compensated for the heat the device itself produces.

buildSteps.title: Write the control firmware
buildSteps.detail: Implement relay timing that protects the compressor, stage logic for multi-stage equipment, and fail-safe defaults so a network outage never leaves the house without heat.

buildSteps.title: Build the learning layer
buildSteps.detail: Combine motion history, light levels and phone location to infer when the home is occupied and asleep, then fit a schedule and setback temperatures to that pattern; a cloud service adds weather forecasts so pre-heating can be scheduled ahead of a cold morning.

buildSteps.title: Add connectivity and reporting
buildSteps.detail: Pair the unit with a phone app over Wi-Fi, expose usage history, and enrol it in utility demand-response programmes where the homeowner opts in.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture and test
buildSteps.detail: Surface-mount the boards, assemble the case and mounting plate, then run each unit through a functional test that exercises every output and confirms calibration.

buildSteps.title: Install and commission
buildSteps.detail: The installer or homeowner moves the existing wires to the matching terminals, the unit detects the equipment type from the wiring, and a setup wizard confirms the first heating and cooling cycles work.

buildSteps.title: Operate and update
buildSteps.detail: Firmware and models are improved remotely over the life of the device, and the cloud service keeps running the scheduling and reporting.

prerequisites.why: interoperability with existing furnaces and air conditioners is what allows a thermostat to be swapped in without rewiring a house.
remote control, weather-aware scheduling and usage reporting all depend on it.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap MEMS sensors and accurate digital thermistors
prerequisites.why: occupancy and temperature sensing must cost only a few dollars to fit a mass-market product.

prerequisites.tech: Machine learning small enough for embedded and cloud use
prerequisites.why: occupancy prediction is what separates a learning thermostat from a programmable one.

prerequisites.tech: Time-of-use tariffs and utility demand-response programmes
prerequisites.why: without them the thermostat cannot shift heating to cheaper or cleaner hours or earn its owner anything for helping the grid.

pathway.milestone: learning thermostats widely installed in single-zone homes
pathway.unlocks: automatic setback in empty houses and clear energy reporting in an app.

pathway.milestone: room-by-room control with wireless remote sensors and motorised vents or dampers
pathway.unlocks: heating and cooling only the rooms in use, which conventional single-zone systems cannot do.

pathway.milestone: native control of heat pumps and flexible tariffs
pathway.unlocks: running the heat pump when electricity is cheapest and lowest-carbon, instead of on a fixed schedule.

pathway.milestone: aggregated fleets of thermostats bidding into grid markets, coordinated with home solar and batteries
pathway.unlocks: households paid for helping balance the grid, and less need for peaking generation.
